classification.difficultyReason: Connect specified intersections and a common-axis trigonometric sketch to an exact integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show by substitution that $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos 2x$ meet at $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.short: At $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, both functions equal $-1$. At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, both functions equal $\dfrac12$.
answer.worked:
At $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&=-1,\\\cos\left(2\times-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&=\cos(-\pi)\\&=-1.\end{align*}$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin\frac{\pi}{6}&=\frac12,\\\cos\left(2\times\frac{\pi}{6}\right)&=\cos\frac{\pi}{3}\\&=\frac12.\end{align*}$$
The two functions have the same value at each specified $x$-coordinate, so they meet at both points.

The supplied equation-solving working also gives:
$$\begin{align*}\sin x&=\cos 2x\\\sin x&=1-2\sin^2x\\2\sin^2x+\sin x-1&=0\\(2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\sin x=\dfrac12$ or $\sin x=-1$, giving $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ respectively in the interval used in part b.

children.label: b
children.prompt: On the same number plane, sketch $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos 2x$, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.short: The curves meet at $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac12\right)$. Between these points, $y=\cos 2x$ lies above $y=\sin x$. See sketch.
answer.worked: $y=\sin x$ increases from $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-1\right)$ through $(0,0)$ to $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac12\right)$. The curve $y=\cos 2x$ rises from the first intersection to its maximum $(0,1)$, then falls to the second intersection. Draw both curves on the same axes.

children.prompt: Hence find the area of the region bounded by the two curves.
